vignette: At 74 years old, Aroha found himself grappling with the shadows of a past he had long tried to escape. Having spent decades as an editor, he was accustomed to scrutinizing the words of others, yet he now felt unbearably vulnerable when faced with critique. This sensitivity stemmed from a traumatic relationship with a former partner, who had subjected him to physical and emotional abuse. Aroha remembered that time not as a continuous narrative but as fragmented snapshots — brief, haunting moments that replayed in his mind like a film stuck on a loop. Each image transported him back to a place where he felt utterly powerless, triggering an intense rage that bubbled beneath the surface. The mere thought of being criticized, whether in his professional life or personal interactions, would send him spiraling into panic, compelling him to avoid those situations at all costs. He started declining invitations to meetings and social gatherings, convinced that even the possibility of receiving feedback would be too overwhelming to handle. Each time he turned down an invitation, the memories of his abuser resurfaced, compelling him to avoid situations where he might face criticism, reinforcing his belief that he was fragile and could not cope with the emotional fallout. These memories became triggers that set off a cascade of avoidance; he would tell himself that staying home was the safest option, believing it was better to miss out than risk encountering anything that could remind him of that painful past. In his daily life, Aroha began to navigate his world with an ever-growing sense of dread. Whenever he encountered something that reminded him of his abuser — a particular gesture, a tone of voice, or even the sight of someone who bore a resemblance — he felt an instinctive urge to withdraw. He would distract himself with work, burying himself in editing tasks to drown out the memories that threatened to surface. This avoidance became a strategy to sidestep the emotional turmoil, but it only served to amplify the urgency of the memories, making them feel more immediate and intrusive whenever he allowed himself a moment of stillness. Yet, with each act of avoidance, he quietly accepted the notion that he must be weaker than he had assumed, collecting proof through his behaviors that he couldn't cope with life as it once was. Yet, this avoidance led to an ironic consequence: the more he pushed those memories away, the more they loomed in his mind, distorting his perception of reality. In his attempts to distract himself from these memories, he immersed himself in work, believing that if he kept busy enough, he could stave off the emotional chaos that awaited him, but this only served to reinforce the memories' urgency and intrusiveness. He had come to believe he was no longer capable of feeling normal emotions, that he had become an object rather than a person deserving of kindness. This negative appraisal fed into the memories of his trauma, making them more vivid as he unconsciously sought evidence of his perceived failure in the moments he replayed — each recollection reinforcing his belief that he was fundamentally broken. This negative appraisal made the memories of his trauma more pronounced, as he often found himself fixating on moments that reaffirmed his perceived inadequacies and failures. He believed that he must have been weak to have allowed the abuse to happen, which made the intrusive memories feel more vivid, as if they were proof of his shortcomings, and thus easier to access whenever he felt threatened. This conviction shaped his intrusive memories, as he often found himself replaying moments of the trauma, convinced that they were evidence of his fundamental flaws and weaknesses. This sense of dehumanization only deepened his isolation, reinforcing his tendency to shy away from those who might inadvertently trigger memories of his trauma. His belief that he was no longer capable of normal emotions made the memories of the traumatic events even more vivid and intrusive, as if they were constantly waiting to remind him of his perceived inadequacies. Aroha's recollections of the traumatic events felt increasingly alien — as if they belonged to someone else entirely. He would hear himself recounting the stories, but they felt detached, like watching a film instead of living through the pain. Each time he recalled the violence, the memories would drive him to distract himself through work, believing that burying the past would protect him from reliving those haunting moments. Each time he recalled the violence, he felt the rage swell within him anew, a visceral response that frightened him. The intensity of these memories drove him to distract himself with work, believing that any moment of stillness would inevitably lead him back to the emotional chaos he was desperately trying to escape. The more he struggled with those memories, the more he felt compelled to withdraw from social situations, fearing that confronting them would only intensify his emotional pain. His memories, instead of fading with time, seemed to tighten their grip on him, making it harder to let go. The more he tried to distract himself from these recollections, the more they intruded upon his thoughts, like unwelcome guests at a dinner party. He found himself trapped in a vicious cycle where his efforts to avoid feelings only intensified the memories, leading him back to the triggers that haunted him. Whenever he was reminded of his abuser, the anxiety surged within him, compelling him to avoid social situations altogether, convinced that the discomfort of facing those triggers was unbearable. Over the years, Aroha's social interactions dwindled. Each place he avoided became a daily reminder of his trauma, reinforcing a map of maladaptive strategies that only deepened his sense of isolation and further etched the boundaries of his world. He avoided gatherings where he might face criticism or run into anyone who reminded him of his past. Each place he avoided became a daily reminder of his trauma, mapping out a life filled with restrictions that only served to deepen his sense of isolation and vulnerability. This avoidance not only limited his social interactions but also formed a network of reminders — places he no longer visited and faces he actively neglected — which continuously echoed the trauma he sought to escape. The loneliness was palpable, yet it felt safer than risking the emotional upheaval that came with engaging with others. He was certain that by keeping his distance, he was protecting himself from further pain, but this strategy only reinforced his negative self-assessments. He felt like a shell of his former self, believing that the trauma had permanently altered his ability to connect with others. This belief lingered in his mind, drawing him back to episodes of the trauma, as if to affirm his conviction that he was no longer worthy of connection or intimacy. Each act of avoidance reinforced this belief, as he internalized the message that he was fragile and needed to keep his distance to protect his already shattered self-image. The more he engaged in these avoidance behaviors, the more he felt that he was confirming his own fragility, leading him to believe that he was incapable of confronting the emotional turmoil stemming from his past. Each act of avoidance reinforced his belief that he was fragile, convincing him that he needed to continue isolating himself to protect his already shattered self-image. Each time he engaged in avoidance behaviors, he internalized the message that he was fragile, reinforcing his negative self-assessment that he could no longer cope with life as he once had. Each day was a reminder of the lost emotions he feared he would never reclaim. Now, as he sat in the dim light of his living room surrounded by the remnants of his once-vibrant life, Aroha felt the weight of his choices. The walls felt like they were closing in, and he was haunted by the thought that he would remain trapped in this cycle forever. It was this realization that finally nudged him toward seeking help. He feared the process of unearthing those buried memories, worried that he might not survive the emotions that awaited him. Yet, a flicker of hope emerged alongside his fear — the hope that perhaps, in confronting his past, he might reclaim a sense of wholeness he thought long lost.
